```{python}
import polars as pl
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn import metrics
# add the additional libraries you need to import for ML here
from xgboost import XGBClassifier, XGBRegressor
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)
```


```{python}
# import your data here using polars and the URL
dwellings_url = "https://github.com/byuidatascience/data4dwellings/raw/master/data-raw/dwellings_ml/dwellings_ml.csv"
neighborhoods_url = "https://github.com/byuidatascience/data4dwellings/raw/master/data-raw/dwellings_neighborhoods_ml/dwellings_neighborhoods_ml.csv"

dwellings_ml = pl.read_csv(dwellings_url)
neighborhoods_ml = pl.read_csv(neighborhoods_url)

# Same random state everywhere so results are reproducible
RANDOM_STATE = 42
TEST_SIZE = 0.2  # matches Task 3 (80/20 split, stratified)
```

## QUESTION 1

1. __Join the `dwellings_neighborhoods_ml.csv` data to the `dwelling_ml.csv` on the `parcel` column to create a new dataset. Duplicate the code for the model you recommended in the previous task above and update it to use this data. Explain the differences and if this changes the model you recommend to the Client.__

After filtering out exact duplicates the number of rows stays the same but the number of columns significantly increases by more than 6 times. This increase in features gives the model a lot more to chew on.

The increase in distinguishing features also increased the model's accuracy. So I'd recommend the same model just trained on the new dataset instead of the old. Especially since out of the top 10 features used, 4 of them were from the neighborhoods data.

```{python}
# --- Check the join key before joining ---
# Both files repeat some parcels (a house can sell more than once).
# The neighborhoods file has exact duplicate rows, so joining it as-is
# would multiply rows. Remove those duplicates first.
key_check = pl.DataFrame({
    "dataset": ["dwellings_ml", "neighborhoods_ml"],
    "rows": [dwellings_ml.height, neighborhoods_ml.height],
    "unique_parcels": [dwellings_ml["parcel"].n_unique(), neighborhoods_ml["parcel"].n_unique()],
    "rows_after_dropping_exact_duplicates": [dwellings_ml.unique().height, neighborhoods_ml.unique().height],
})
key_check
```

```{python}
neighborhoods_unique = neighborhoods_ml.unique()

dwellings_joined = dwellings_ml.join(neighborhoods_unique, on="parcel", how="inner")

print(f"Original rows: {dwellings_ml.height:,} | Joined rows: {dwellings_joined.height:,}")
print(f"Original columns: {dwellings_ml.width} | Joined columns: {dwellings_joined.width}")
```

```{python}
# --- Same XGBoost model recommended in Task 3, run on both datasets ---
# Identical settings on both, so any difference comes from the data, not the model
def fit_classifier(df):
    X = df.drop(["parcel", "yrbuilt", "before1980"])
    y = df["before1980"]
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
        X.to_pandas(), y.to_pandas(), test_size=TEST_SIZE, stratify=y.to_pandas(),
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE
    )
    model = XGBClassifier(
        n_estimators=400,
        learning_rate=0.1,
        max_depth=6,
        subsample=0.8,
        colsample_bytree=0.8,
        eval_metric="logloss",
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
        n_jobs=-1,
    )
    model.fit(X_train, y_train.astype(int))
    return model, X_test, y_test, model.predict(X_test)

clf_orig, Xte_orig, yte_orig, pred_orig = fit_classifier(dwellings_ml)
clf_join, Xte_join, yte_join, pred_join = fit_classifier(dwellings_joined)

comparison = pl.DataFrame({
    "dataset": ["Original (dwellings_ml)", "Joined (+ neighborhoods)"],
    "features": [Xte_orig.shape[1], Xte_join.shape[1]],
    "accuracy": [metrics.accuracy_score(yte_orig, pred_orig), metrics.accuracy_score(yte_join, pred_join)],
    "precision": [metrics.precision_score(yte_orig, pred_orig), metrics.precision_score(yte_join, pred_join)],
    "recall": [metrics.recall_score(yte_orig, pred_orig), metrics.recall_score(yte_join, pred_join)],
    "f1": [metrics.f1_score(yte_orig, pred_orig), metrics.f1_score(yte_join, pred_join)],
}).with_columns(pl.col(["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1"]).round(4))
comparison
```

```{python}
print("Classification report - joined data")
print(metrics.classification_report(yte_join, pred_join, target_names=["1980 or later", "Before 1980"]))
```

```{python}
# Permutation importance on the joined model (top 10 features)
# max_samples=2000 scores on a random subset of the test set so this runs in
# seconds instead of minutes with 300+ columns
perm_join = permutation_importance(
    clf_join, Xte_join, yte_join, n_repeats=5, max_samples=2000,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=1
)
imp_join = (
    pl.DataFrame({"feature": Xte_join.columns, "importance": perm_join.importances_mean})
    .sort("importance", descending=True)
    .head(10)
)

(
    ggplot(imp_join, aes(x="importance", y="feature"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="#2a6f97")
    + scale_y_discrete(limits=imp_join["feature"].reverse().to_list())
    + labs(
        title="Top 10 features - joined data (permutation importance)",
        x="Mean drop in accuracy when shuffled",
        y="",
    )
    + theme_minimal()
)
```

```{python}
# How many neighborhood columns made the top 10?
imp_join.with_columns(pl.col("feature").str.starts_with("nbhd_").alias("is_neighborhood"))
```


## QUESTION 2

1. __Can you build a model that predicts the year a house was built? Note this is a regression ML model, not a classifier. Report appropriate evaluation metrics for the model. Explain the model and the evaluation metrics you used to determine if the model is good.__

I measured the accuracy of the regression model with a couple things first. I compared how it held up against a baseline mean year prediction. The Mean Absolute Error for the model was 8.69 years per house, whereas the Root Mean Squared Error which gives more weight to big mistakes was around 14.5 which means there were a few predictions that were way off. R squared which is the coefficient of determination shows that the model explains around 85% of the variation.

Another measure of accuracy is I tested to see what percentage of predictions made fell within an accuracy of within 5, 10, and 20 years of the actual construction date. The model had about 90% of homes at least within 20 years of the actual construction date.

We can see also based on the graphs of predicted vs actual year built and prediction error by actual year built that most of the large errors on average come from the oldest homes while newer homes are more accurately predicted.

Overall if the client wants a predicted year of construction I do think the regression model would work, but the classifier is still more accurate so if that's not a requirement I'd go with that.

```{python}
# --- Regression: predict yrbuilt ---
# Drop before1980 too: it is derived from yrbuilt and would leak the answer.
X_reg = dwellings_joined.drop(["parcel", "yrbuilt", "before1980"])
y_reg = dwellings_joined["yrbuilt"]

Xr_train, Xr_test, yr_train, yr_test = train_test_split(
    X_reg.to_pandas(), y_reg.to_pandas(), test_size=TEST_SIZE,
    stratify=dwellings_joined["before1980"].to_pandas(),  # keep the pre/post-1980 mix even in train and test
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)

# Same XGBoost settings as the classifier; only the objective changes
# (squared error on the year instead of log loss on before/after 1980)
reg = XGBRegressor(
    n_estimators=400,
    learning_rate=0.1,
    max_depth=6,
    subsample=0.8,
    colsample_bytree=0.8,
    objective="reg:squarederror",
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    n_jobs=-1,
)
reg.fit(Xr_train, yr_train)
yr_pred = reg.predict(Xr_test)

# Baseline: always guess the average year from the training data.
# A useful model has to beat this.
baseline_pred = np.full(len(yr_test), yr_train.mean())

reg_metrics = pl.DataFrame({
    "model": ["Baseline (predict mean year)", "XGBoost Regressor"],
    "MAE (years)": [metrics.mean_absolute_error(yr_test, baseline_pred), metrics.mean_absolute_error(yr_test, yr_pred)],
    "RMSE (years)": [metrics.root_mean_squared_error(yr_test, baseline_pred), metrics.root_mean_squared_error(yr_test, yr_pred)],
    "R2": [metrics.r2_score(yr_test, baseline_pred), metrics.r2_score(yr_test, yr_pred)],
}).with_columns(pl.col(["MAE (years)", "RMSE (years)", "R2"]).round(3))
reg_metrics
```

```{python}
# Share of predictions within N years of the true year (easy to explain to a client)
abs_err = np.abs(yr_test.to_numpy() - yr_pred)
pl.DataFrame({
    "within": ["5 years", "10 years", "20 years"],
    "share_of_homes": [np.mean(abs_err <= 5), np.mean(abs_err <= 10), np.mean(abs_err <= 20)],
}).with_columns(pl.col("share_of_homes").round(3))
```

```{python}
# Predicted vs actual
pred_df = pl.DataFrame({"actual": yr_test.to_numpy(), "predicted": yr_pred})

(
    ggplot(pred_df, aes(x="actual", y="predicted"))
    + geom_point(alpha=0.15, color="#2a6f97", size=1.5)
    + geom_abline(intercept=0, slope=1, color="#c0392b", linetype="dashed")
    + geom_vline(xintercept=1980, color="gray", linetype="dotted")
    + scale_x_continuous(format="d")  # plain years, no thousands comma
    + scale_y_continuous(format="d")
    + labs(
        title="Predicted vs actual year built",
        subtitle="Dashed line = perfect prediction; dotted line = 1980",
        x="Actual year built",
        y="Predicted year built",
    )
    + theme_minimal()
)
```

```{python}
# Residuals: where does the model miss?
pred_df = pred_df.with_columns((pl.col("predicted") - pl.col("actual")).alias("residual"))

(
    ggplot(pred_df, aes(x="actual", y="residual"))
    + geom_point(alpha=0.15, color="#2a6f97", size=1.5)
    + geom_hline(yintercept=0, color="#c0392b", linetype="dashed")
    + scale_x_continuous(format="d")  # plain years, no thousands comma
    + labs(
        title="Prediction error by actual year built",
        x="Actual year built",
        y="Predicted - actual (years)",
    )
    + theme_minimal()
)
```

```{python}
# Bonus: use the regression model as a classifier for the client's real question
reg_as_clf = (yr_pred < 1980).astype(int)
true_clf = (yr_test.to_numpy() < 1980).astype(int)
print("Regression predictions turned into before/after 1980:")
print(metrics.classification_report(true_clf, reg_as_clf, target_names=["1980 or later", "Before 1980"]))
```
